page:
Lifecycle events for request-response handling in multiple stages. Lifecycle divided into events: request, parse, transform, derive, beforeHandle, resolve, afterHandle, mapResponse, error, afterResponse. Designed to separate process into distinct phases based on responsibility without interference. Lifecycle follows specific order - visualization available at /assets/lifecycle-chart.svg.
Questions: What are lifecycle events? Why divide into phases? What is the execution order?

sections.manifest:
Lifecycle purpose: separate concerns into distinct phases. Example: detect HTML response and set Content-Type header automatically. Eliminates need to set header on every route. Lifecycle hooks apply automatically.
Questions: Why use lifecycle events? What problems do they solve?

Hook types: Local Hook (specific route), Interceptor Hook (every route after registration). Inline hook into route or use .on<Event> methods. Hook accepts same Context as handler.
Questions: What hook types exist? How do you use them?

Local hooks in route options. Example: get('/', () => 'html', { afterHandle({ responseValue, set }) { if isHtml(responseValue) set.headers['Content-Type'] = 'text/html; charset=utf8' } }). Affects single route. Response /: text/html, /hi: text/plain.
Questions: How do local hooks work? When do they apply?

Interceptor hooks via .on<Event> methods. Example: .onAfterHandle(). Applies to every handler after hook registration for current instance. All routes: /none, /, /hi. Route before hook: text/plain. Routes after hook: text/html.
Questions: How do interceptor hooks work? Which routes do they affect?

Order of code critical for lifecycle application. Events apply to routes AFTER registration. Put onError before plugin, plugin won't inherit onError. Console log 1 before route, 2 after - only 1 logs. Same applies to plugins. Exception: onRequest - global event independent of route.
Questions: Why does order matter? What is exception? How does onRequest differ?

Request event - first lifecycle event for every request. Provides minimal context to reduce overhead. Recommended scenarios: caching, rate limiter/IP lock, analytic, provide custom headers (CORS). PreContext with attributes: request (Request), set (Set), store, decorators. No derived value. Returning value uses response, skips rest of lifecycle.
Questions: When is onRequest executed? What context does it provide? When should you use it?

Parse event - body parser equivalent. Parses body; return value appends to Context.body. Continues iterating through parsers until body assigned or all executed. Default parsers: text/plain, application/json, multipart/form-data, application/x-www-form-urlencoded. Use onParse for custom body parser. Context adds contentType property. Example custom: if contentType === 'application/custom-type' return request.text().
Questions: What does parse do? What default parsers exist? How do you add custom parser?

Body parser selection ahead of time. Elysia determines body function by reading body type. Criteria: application/json if t.Object, multipart/form-data if t.Object 1-level deep with t.File, application/x-www-form-urlencoded if t.URLEncoded, text/plain for other primitives. Specify explicitly via parse shorthand: 'json', 'formdata', 'urlencoded', 'text', 'none', or full content-type. Skip parsing via parse: 'none' for third-party libraries (tRPC, orpc) where Body already used.
Questions: How does Elysia pick parser? What parse options exist? When skip parsing?

Custom parser registration. Use .parser('name', ({ request, contentType }) => ...return value...). Apply in parse via array: ['custom', 'json']. Multiple parsers attempted sequentially.
Questions: How do you register custom parsers?

Transform event - mutate context before validation. Recommended for: mutating existing context, derive based on onTransform with type support. Example: mutate params to numeric values via +params.id.
Questions: What does transform do? When should you use it?

Derive event - append new value to context before validation. Assigned once per request (unlike state/decorate assigned at startup). Can access Request properties: headers, query, body. Values unique per request, not shared. Recommend using resolve instead in most cases - executes after validation making it more secure.
Questions: When is derive assigned? What can it access? When use resolve instead?

Derive and transform queue. Both stored in same stack. onTransform executes first, then derive in same queue. Execution order shown in console log.
Questions: What queue order is used? How do derive and transform interact?

BeforeHandle event - after validation, before handler. Custom validation for specific requirements. Return value skips handler. Recommended for: restricted access (authorization, sign-in), custom request requirements. Example: check validateSession(session.value), return status(401) if invalid. Response: signed in -> Hi, not signed in -> Unauthorized.
Questions: When is beforeHandle executed? What can it do? When return value?

Guard for multiple beforeHandle application. Apply same beforeHandle to multiple routes. Example: guard({ beforeHandle: isSignIn }, (app) => app.get().post()). Creates encapsulated scope for beforeHandle.
Questions: What is guard? How do you use it?

Resolve event - append value after validation. Identical syntax to derive. Stored in same stack as beforeHandle. Executes after validation so more secure. Example: extract bearer from Authorization header. Guard resolve for encapsulation.
Questions: When does resolve execute? Why more secure than derive? How guard resolve?

AfterHandle event - after main handler, map returned value to proper response. Recommended for: transform requests into new value (compression, event stream), add custom headers based on response (Content-Type). Return value used as new response unless undefined. Iteration continues unlike beforeHandle. Example: detect HTML response, set content-type header.
Questions: When is afterHandle executed? What can it transform? When return value?

MapResponse event - after afterHandle, custom response mapping. Recommended for: compression, map value into Web Standard Response. Example: gzip compression via Bun.gzipSync, set Content-Encoding header, return new Response. After return value, next mapResponse iteration skipped. Elysia auto-merges set.headers - no manual append needed.
Questions: When is mapResponse executed? What transformations are common?

OnError event - error handling for lifecycle errors. Executes when error thrown in any lifecycle. Recommended for: custom error messages, fail-safe handling/retry, logging/analytics. Elysia catches all handler errors, classifies error code, pipes to onError. Example: return new Response(error.toString()). Must register before handler to apply. Error code examples: NOT_FOUND, PARSE, VALIDATION, INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR, INVALID_COOKIE_SIGNATURE, INVALID_FILE_TYPE, UNKNOWN, number (HTTP status). If no response returned, uses error.name.
Questions: When is onError executed? What error codes exist? When return response?

Local error handling via guard. Scope error handler to specific routes via guard. Example: get('/', handler, { beforeHandle, error() { return 'Handled' } }).
Questions: How do you scope error handling?

AfterResponse event - after response sent to client. Recommended for: clean up response, logging/analytics. Example: log performance.now(). Similar to mapResponse, accepts responseValue (value returned from handler, not Web Response). Access set for headers/status returned. Does not require return value.
Questions: When is afterResponse executed? What cleanup can you do? Why use it?
